target.title: Decoding Imagined and Spoken Phrases From Non-invasive Neural (MEG) Signals
target.version: Original Research; Frontiers in Neuroscience 14:290 (published version)

read.pdf: No local PDF supplied; Tables 1–2 consulted in PMC full-text HTML; figures not visually inspected.

entries.text: The study reports feasibility of five-class decoding of imagined and overt phrases from single-trial non-invasive MEG.
entries.condition: Eight adult subjects; five phrase classes; single-trial MEG; imagined/preparatory and overt-production conditions.

entries.text: The dataset comprised 8 subjects, 5 phrase stimuli, and 100 repetitions per stimulus: 4,000 recorded trials, of which 3,046 were retained; the paper reports about 75 valid trials per phrase per subject.
entries.unit: subjects; phrase classes; trials per stimulus; recorded trials; retained trials; retained trials per phrase per subject, respectively
entries.condition: After visual artifact and timing-compliance exclusions; one trial is a phrase presentation/response sequence.
entries.quote: a total of 3, 046 valid trials were retained out of 4, 000

entries.text: The five class labels were AAC-style English phrases: Do you understand me; That's perfect; How are you; Good-bye; I need help.
entries.condition: Phrases displayed as stimuli; subjects covertly read, imagined/prepared, then overtly articulated each phrase.

entries.text: Each trial included 0.5 s pre-stimulus, 1 s perception, 1 s preparation/imagination, and natural-rate articulation averaging 2 s; the next trial followed a 1–1.5 s baseline.
entries.unit: seconds (pre-stimulus; perception; preparation; mean articulation; inter-trial baseline)
entries.condition: Delayed overt reading protocol; articulation duration varied by subject (1.5 s for one, 2 s for two, 2.5 s for five subjects).
entries.quote: The pre-stimuli segment was designated as a period of 0.5 s prior to the stimulus onset.

entries.text: The decoder used 196 of the 204 gradiometer sensors; eight noisy/artifact-like sensors were excluded.
entries.condition: Only planar gradiometers were used for decoding; exclusions were across subjects where channels were noisy or irregular.

entries.text: The analyzed MEG was low-pass filtered below 250 Hz with a fourth-order Butterworth filter; preprocessed signals were at 1 kHz.
entries.unit: Hz cutoff; filter order; kHz sampling frequency after preprocessing
entries.condition: Valid, artifact-screened gradiometer trials; the supplied text reports the post-preprocessing sampling frequency.

entries.text: Denoising used a seven-level Daubechies db-4 DWT; detail components above 125 Hz were discarded, and remaining bands were reconstructed for analysis.
entries.condition: The paper describes d1/d2 rejection and reconstruction of high-gamma, gamma, beta, alpha, theta, and delta bands.

entries.text: The ANN used a 1,176-dimensional concatenation of RMS features across six reconstructed frequency bands and 196 sensors.
entries.condition: One RMS value per sensor per band; the six bands were high-gamma, gamma, beta, alpha, theta, and delta.

entries.text: RMS was selected as the ANN feature after testing statistical features; its class difference was significant by one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey.
entries.condition: Five phrase classes; the text does not identify whether feature screening was restricted to training data.

entries.text: The ANN was a shallow single-hidden-layer network with 256 randomized hidden weights/nodes, sigmoid transformation, softmax, and five-class output; weights were updated by back-propagation with SGD.
entries.condition: ANN baseline on RMS features for five phrase classes.

entries.text: ANN learning rate was tuned on validation data across 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, and 0.0001; 0.01 was selected.
entries.condition: Coarse-to-fine validation-data tuning for the ANN baseline.

entries.text: The ANN used three separate random train/validation/test splits; early stopping was based on validation loss, with maximum 100 epochs and overfitting often beginning around 35 epochs.
entries.value: 3 splits; >6 epochs of increasing validation loss; 100 maximum epochs; approximately 35 epochs to overfit
entries.condition: Each split was 70% training, 15% validation, 15% test; no random seed was reported.
entries.quote: we performed ANN training on three separate random splits to find the average performance.

entries.text: Three ImageNet-pretrained CNNs were evaluated: AlexNet, ResNet101, and Inception-ResNet-v2; their final classification layers were adapted to five phrase classes.
entries.value: 3 architectures; 5 output classes; pretrained on >1 million images and 1,000 categories
entries.condition: Transfer learning; initial layers retained while final task-specific layers were replaced.
entries.quote: namely AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., ), ResNet101 (Wu et al., ), and Inception-ResNet-v2 (Szegedy et al., )

entries.text: CNN inputs were Morlet CWT scalograms; ST-CNN used per-sensor spectral-temporal images, while SST-CNN packed the 196 sensors into a 14 × 14 image.
entries.condition: The ST-CNN single-trial score averaged cross-entropy across 196 sensor scalograms; SST-CNN used one spatial-spectral-temporal image per trial.
entries.quote: we created a 14 × 14 matrix of scalogram images (obtained from 196 sensors) within a single image

entries.text: SST-CNN data augmentation shifted signals positively by 100 and 200 ms, tripling input size; original trials and augmentations remained within the same partition.
entries.condition: Augmentation was used for SST-CNN only; ST-CNN and ANN were not augmented. The authors cite approximately 250 ms average speech-production reaction time as motivation for the shifts.
entries.quote: A linear positive shift of both 100 and 200 ms was performed on the signals and then their scalogram images were generated.

entries.text: CNN image inputs were resized to AlexNet 227 × 227 × 3, ResNet101 224 × 224 × 3, and Inception-ResNet-v2 299 × 299 × 3.
entries.condition: Color scalogram images; model-specific input-size requirements.

entries.text: CNN training used learning rate 0.0001, Adam, minibatch 64, validation frequency/patience 6, maximum 60 epochs, gradient clipping, and otherwise architecture defaults.
entries.unit: learning rate; minibatch examples; validation frequency/patience; epochs
entries.condition: CNNs trained on the paper's 70/15/15 train/validation/test partitions on a 7-GPU Linux (Ubuntu 16.04) server using Keras imported to Matlab 2018b.

entries.text: Train/validation/test partitions were 70%/15%/15%; validation data were used for hyperparameter tuning and overfitting checks, and the test trials were described as unseen.
entries.unit: percent of the whole data (training; validation; testing)
entries.condition: Subject-dependent partitions; testing excluded augmented copies of training and validation trials.
entries.quote: The testing data were completely unseen (without containing any augmented version of the training or validation trials) and hence were new to the model.

entries.text: Training and test examples came from the same subjects/speakers but were unique trials; evaluation was subject-dependent rather than speaker-independent.
entries.condition: No held-out-subject evaluation; authors say learned CNN features may be subject-specific.

entries.text: Random seeds and the exact random split assignments are not reported; ANN averages three random splits, while the architecture table reports three independent runs.
entries.condition: Reproducibility of ANN initialization, partition generation, and CNN runs cannot be reconstructed from the paper text.
entries.quote: we performed ANN training on three separate random splits to find the average performance.

entries.text: The paper does not report a subject/session-level partition or the number of recording sessions used for train/validation/test; the split is described only as percentages of whole data.
entries.condition: Train/test subject overlap is explicit, but session- or site-held-out generalization is not described.

entries.text: The paper does not say whether the ANOVA/Tukey feature screening that selected RMS was performed using training data only or included validation/test examples.
entries.condition: Feature screening preceded the described train/validation/test model fitting; the screening partition is unspecified.

entries.text: No per-sensor, per-subject, or per-trial normalization/scaling procedure for RMS inputs or scalogram image values is specified.
entries.condition: The paper reports filtering, wavelet transforms, color scalograms, and resizing, but no normalization rule beyond these operations.

entries.text: The model performed five-class phrase classification; its reported output was a phrase-class prediction, not reconstructed open-vocabulary text or synthesized speech.
entries.condition: Whole phrases were the classes; the study did not test a speech synthesizer or open-vocabulary decoder.

entries.text: ANN mean accuracy across eight subjects was 71.95% perception, 80.83% imagination/preparation, and 90.55% production; Sec. 4.1 does not give the ANN pre-stimulus mean numerically.
entries.condition: ANN baseline; five-class subject-dependent decoding; average across eight subjects; per-subject test split 15% of trials, with three separate random splits.

entries.text: ST-CNN mean accuracy across eight subjects was 86.83% perception, 91.71% preparation/imagination, and 93.56% production.
entries.condition: Spectral-temporal CNN; five-class subject-dependent decoding; average across eight subjects; 70/15/15 partitioning.
entries.quote: The average classification accuracies obtained with ST-CNN during perception, preparation, and production were 86.83 ± 2.93%, 91.71 ± 1.67%, and 93.56 ± 1.92%, respectively

entries.text: SST-CNN mean accuracy across eight subjects was 90.38% perception, 93.24% preparation/imagination, and 96.65% production.
entries.condition: Spatial-spectral-temporal CNN; five-class subject-dependent decoding; average across eight subjects; 70/15/15 partitioning; input augmented by within-partition 100/200-ms shifts.
entries.quote: whereas, with SST-CNN the accuracies were 90.38 ± 2.28%, 93.24 ± 2.87%, and 96.65 ± 2.88%.

entries.text: The abstract rounds the maximum average accuracy to 93% imagined and 96% spoken phrases; the detailed SST-CNN preparation and production means are 93.24% and 96.65%.
entries.condition: Abstract headline for five phrase classes from single-trial MEG in eight adult subjects; detailed stage-specific values appear in Sec. 4.1.
entries.quote: CNNs were found to be highly effective with an average decoding accuracy of up to 93% for the imagined and 96% for the spoken phrases.

entries.text: All four task stages for ANN and CNNs were reported above 30% chance by one-tailed t-tests at p < 0.05; pre-stimulus accuracy was also above chance at p = 0.00013.
entries.unit: chance accuracy; one-tailed t-test threshold; one-tailed p-value for pre-stimulus vs chance
entries.condition: Five-class classification; reported finite-sample chance level; all methods/stages for the general comparison, with the pre-stimulus result separately specified.
entries.quote: The decoding performances during all the four stages (pre-stimuli, perception, preparation/imagination, articulation) obtained with ANN or CNNs were significantly higher than the chance level accuracy (30%)

entries.text: The authors state the theoretical pre-stimulus chance level is about 30% for N ≈ 300 (about 60 trials × 5 classes), versus 20% for an ideal population size.
entries.unit: % chance; approximate N; trials; classes; % ideal-population chance
entries.condition: Pre-stimulus segment; no stimulus/task; finite-sample chance rationale cited to Combrisson and Jerbi.
entries.quote: about 30% for N = ~300 (~ 60 trials × 5 classes) (Combrisson and Jerbi, ) (20% is for ideal population size)

entries.text: ANN, ST-CNN, and SST-CNN pairwise accuracy comparisons were significant at p < 0.05; the largest reported pairwise p was 0.0099 for ANN versus ST-CNN in production.
entries.condition: Pairwise decoding-performance comparisons among three approaches; production-stage ANN vs ST-CNN is the highest-p comparison.

entries.text: SST-CNN outperformed ST-CNN significantly for all compared stages except preparation, where the two feature approaches did not differ significantly (p = 0.2135).
entries.condition: Comparison of spectral-temporal and spatial-spectral-temporal CNN results; preparation/imagination is the exception.
entries.quote: during the preparation stage ( p = 0.2135).

entries.text: Across-stage pairwise tests were significant except preparation versus production for ST-CNN (p = 0.0589); pre-stimulus results did not differ significantly among the three methods (p > 0.05).
entries.condition: Pairwise stage comparisons regardless of classifier; pre-stimulus classifier comparisons reported separately.
entries.quote: A slightly higher p -value than the desired confidence ( p = 0.0589) was observed.

entries.unit: % accuracy by stage (pre-stimulus; perception; preparation; production)
entries.condition: Five-class SST-CNN; subject-wise results across eight subjects; Table 1 note says test accuracies are averaged over three independent runs across subjects.
entries.quote: shows a comparison of the three specific CNN architectures, where AlexNet slightly outperformed ResNet101 and Inception-ResNet-v2 in terms of decoding accuracy.

entries.text: Table 1 reports cross-architecture mean accuracy 42.96/87.70/90.89/94.50% and standard deviation 0.70/2.82/2.81/2.14% for pre-stimulus/perception/preparation/production.
entries.unit: % accuracy by stage (mean across CNN architectures; table SD)
entries.condition: SST-CNN architecture comparison in Table 1; test accuracies averaged over three independent runs across subjects.

entries.text: The AlexNet articulation confusion matrix reports per-phrase accuracy 96.38%, 96.82%, 96.31%, 96.74%, and 97.11%, with an average of 96.67%.
entries.unit: % correct per true phrase class, then mean
entries.condition: Table 2; five phrase classes; articulation; confusion matrix combined across the eight subjects; AlexNet best decoder.

entries.text: The prose reports about 12 misclassifications per phrase and 0.9%, but Table 2 lists 40–51 off-diagonal errors per true phrase row (inference); the table's denominator is unreconciled.
entries.value: prose: 1,382; approximately 12; 0.9%; Table 2 row counts (true phrase × predicted phrase order): [1332,12,19,11,8], [10,1338,14,11,9], [21,8,1331,12,10], [12,15,12,1337,6], [7,12,14,7,1342]; off-diagonal totals 50,44,51,45,40 (inference)
entries.unit: reported test cases; reported misclassified samples per phrase; reported percent; confusion-matrix sample counts
entries.condition: AlexNet articulation confusion matrix across eight subjects; each true-phrase row sums to 1,382, while the article note calls 1,382 the total test trials, leaving overall-versus-per-class denominator unclear.
entries.quote: The average number of misclassified samples per phrase was about 12 in the combined test set (1, 382) of 8 subjects, i.e., 0.9% misclassification per phrase.

entries.text: The authors claim both CNN approaches outperform the ANN baseline for perception, imagination/preparation, and articulation, with SST-CNN generally strongest.
entries.condition: Their comparison is subject-dependent, five-class, same-subject train/test; approaches also differ in feature representation and SST-CNN augmentation.

entries.text: The authors call the whole-brain spatial-spectral-temporal scalogram-image representation a novel strategy for applying CNNs to neural speech decoding.
entries.condition: The stated novelty concerns the representation combining sensor spatial layout with spectral-temporal scalograms.

entries.text: The authors argue that adding spatial information to spectral-temporal features improves decoding and lets CNNs use spatial, spectral, and temporal MEG information.
entries.condition: Inference is drawn from SST-CNN versus ST-CNN results within the same subject-dependent five-phrase task.

entries.text: In a comparison for three subjects against an earlier pilot study, the authors attribute roughly a 2% average ANN accuracy improvement to wavelet decomposition.
entries.condition: Current ANN results for three subjects compared with Dash et al. (2018d) pilot results; not a full-cohort independent benchmark.

entries.text: The authors caution that CNN-versus-ANN comparisons do not isolate feature efficacy because the feature sets differ in content and dimensionality; they intended to compare approaches.
entries.condition: ANN uses RMS vectors; CNN approaches use scalograms, with SST-CNN additionally using spatial organization and augmentation.
entries.quote: a clear interpretation of what aspects of the scalograms led to better performance is not straight forward, because of the inherent differences in the feature sets, in content and dimension.

entries.text: The authors note SST-CNN augmentation may itself have contributed to its higher performance; they did not augment the other approaches.
entries.condition: Augmentation was applied only to SST-CNN; the authors say applying it to ST-CNN might also improve performance but would be time-consuming.
entries.quote: It is possible that the data augmentation used in the SST-CNN approach might have contributed to better performance

entries.text: The ANN used 1,176 features despite only about 250 training samples per subject across five classes; the authors say dimension reduction may improve it.
entries.value: 1,176 features; approximately 250 training samples per subject; 5 classes
entries.condition: ANN training set, subject-dependent; discussion's approximate sample count.

entries.text: The authors acknowledge phrase-duration differences could contribute to classification and plan to control duration in future phrase/phoneme decoding work.
entries.condition: Overt articulation among the five phrases; duration was not experimentally controlled.
entries.quote: While we think this is a caveat of our experimental design, there is reason to be optimistic that the main contribution is from phrase information, not just duration.

entries.text: Residual jaw-motion artifact could contribute to higher production-stage accuracy; the authors cite prior work suggesting MEG contains more information than jaw motion alone.
entries.condition: Overt articulation stage after denoising; jaw movement was not the decoder's stated primary input.

entries.text: The authors note that carryover from previous articulation may persist for seconds and potentially contaminate current pre-stimulus or perception signals.
entries.value: 1–1.5 s inter-trial delay; possible carryover for many seconds
entries.condition: Consecutive trial protocol; authors considered carryover a potential source of interference.
entries.quote: the effect of speech processing may continue in the brain (carryover) even many seconds after the articulation ends.

entries.text: The authors say imagined speech is difficult to verify and that the one-second preparation/imagination interval may contain both preparation and imagination; phonological processes are unresolved.
entries.condition: The task followed on-screen phrase presentation with overt articulation in the same trial; authors call for studies to dissociate processes.
entries.quote: Nevertheless, our paradigm may have a combination of both preparation and imagination within the 1 s duration.

entries.text: The authors warn that same-subject train/test features may be subject-specific and may not generalize across the population; subject normalization/adaptation is left for future work.
entries.condition: No speaker-independent evaluation was performed.

entries.text: The study used healthy subjects only; the authors say evaluation in locked-in/ALS patients is required.
entries.value: 8 adult subjects in the study; patient cohort not tested
entries.condition: Healthy volunteer cohort; no locked-in or ALS participants.

entries.text: The evaluated vocabulary is a five-phrase closed set; the authors reserve arbitrary/open-vocabulary phrases for future study.
entries.condition: Whole-phrase classification, not phoneme-level/open-set decoding.

entries.text: The authors state MEG is currently unsuitable for speech-BCI deployment because of its cost, size, and immobility; wearable OPM-MEG is presented as a future possibility.
entries.condition: No portable device or patient-facing deployment was evaluated in this experiment.

entries.text: No real-time decoding latency, continuous-use test, user communication rate, or online speech-synthesis result is reported; the experiment is offline phrase classification.
entries.condition: The authors discuss faster communication and future BCIs as motivation, but report classifier accuracy rather than online use.

entries.text: No language model, vocabulary prior, or other use-time linguistic aid is described; the task is a closed five-class classifier.
entries.condition: Five phrase classes; no open-vocabulary decoding or language-model-assisted evaluation.

entries.text: No user confirmation, reject option, or confidence-based confirmation behavior is reported.
entries.condition: The study describes five-class decoder outputs and offline accuracy evaluation only.

entries.text: No correction, undo, or online adaptation mechanism is reported after a phrase-class prediction.
entries.condition: Offline five-class decoding; no interactive user correction protocol described.

entries.text: The authors say code can be obtained from the corresponding authors upon request; no public repository is linked.
entries.condition: No code URL in the paper; therefore no repository README or scripts were available for code-condition extraction.

entries.text: The authors cite an earlier ANN study suggesting 40 trials are sufficient for speech decoding before performance saturates; this is prior-work rationale, not the present study's held-out test size.
entries.condition: Prior work cited to justify the present 70/15/15 split; the present paper does not restate that earlier study's full evaluation conditions here.

entries.text: The longest phrase's mean overt-production time was 0.97 ± 0.08 s across trials, cited when discussing the one-second preparation/imagination interval.
